sessions.title: Words and their jobs
sessions.intro: Nouns, pronouns, verbs and adjectives, then the present tenses. Every sentence is one you could hear on a banking, insurance, tourism or BPO call.

sets.title: Nouns
explanation: What it is: A noun is the name of a person, place, thing or idea: customer, branch, card, delay, advice.

Its job: Nouns are the subject or the object of the sentence. The key question on a call is: can I count it? Countable nouns take a/an and a plural -s (a receipt, two receipts). Uncountable nouns take neither (information, advice, luggage, equipment, feedback, money).
examples: Could you share your account number, please?
The claim form is on our website.
Your driver will meet you at the airport.
Thank you for your patience.

sayThis.say: Could I have some information about the policy?
sayThis.why: Information is uncountable: no -s and no “an”.

items.question: Could you send me some more ____ about the home loan?
items.explanation: Information is uncountable: no -s and no “an”.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Let me give you an advice.
Let me give you some advice.
items.explanation: Advice is uncountable. Say some advice or a piece of advice.

items.question: How many ____ are you carrying, sir?
items.explanation: Bag is countable, so the plural is bags. Luggage has no plural.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Thank you for your valuable feedbacks.
Thank you for your valuable feedback.
items.explanation: Feedback is uncountable: no -s.

items.question: Our IT team will replace the faulty ____ today.
items.explanation: Equipment is uncountable: no -s and no “an”.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Please bring all the documents to the branch.
Please bring all the document to the branch.
Please bring all the document's to the branch.
items.explanation: All the + a countable noun takes the plural: documents, with no apostrophe.

items.question: One of our ____ will call you within the hour.
items.explanation: After “one of”, use a plural noun: one of our agents.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We have two vacancy in Colombo.
We have two vacancies in Colombo.
items.explanation: Two + a plural noun. A consonant + y becomes -ies.

items.question: How much ____ do you have with you, madam?
items.explanation: How much + an uncountable noun: luggage. With bags you would ask how many.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The furnitures in the room are new.
The furniture in the room is new.
The furniture in the room are new.
items.explanation: Furniture is uncountable and takes a singular verb: is.

items.question: Our ____ are trained to help you in Sinhala, Tamil and English.
items.explanation: Staff is a group word with no -s. For individual people, say staff members.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I need a few minutes to check your details.
I need a few minute to check your details.
items.explanation: A few + a plural countable noun: minutes.

items.question: The tour includes three ____ at local restaurants.
items.explanation: Three + plural: meals. An apostrophe shows possession, not a plural.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: There was a damage to the roof.
There was some damage to the roof.
There were damages to the roof.
items.explanation: Damage (harm) is uncountable. “Damages” means money a court awards.

items.question: Please keep all your ____ for the claim.
items.explanation: All your + a countable plural: receipts.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
items.explanation: Money is uncountable: no -s and no apostrophe.

items.question: The guide will tell you about the ____ of the temple.
items.explanation: The history of one place is uncountable here.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
items.explanation: Jewellery is uncountable. One ring is “a piece of jewellery”.

items.question: Could we have two ____ of tea, please?
items.explanation: Two + plural: cups. Cups of tea makes uncountable tea countable.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The research shows that most customers prefer chat.
The researches show that most customers prefers chat.
items.explanation: Research is uncountable, and customers (plural) takes prefer.

sets.title: Pronouns
explanation: What it is: A pronoun stands in for a noun so you don't repeat it: I, you, he, she, it, we, they; me, him, her, us, them; my, your, our, yours.

Its job: Subject pronouns (I, he, we) come before the verb. Object pronouns (me, him, us) come after a verb or a preposition. On calls, “you” and “we” keep the conversation personal: we (the company) will help you (the customer).
examples: I'll check that for you now.
We'll send you an SMS when it's done.
Could you give it to me, please?
He said he would call back.

sayThis.say: My name is Kamal. How can I help you?
sayThis.why: Use myself only when the subject and object are the same person: I hurt myself.

items.question: Good morning, ____ Nadeesha from Ceylon Bank.
items.explanation: Introduce yourself with “This is…” or “My name is…”, not “Myself…”.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He said me the card was blocked.
He told me the card was blocked.
He said to me the card blocked.
items.explanation: Tell takes a person (told me). Say does not (he said that…).

items.question: Please send the form to ____ by Friday.
items.explanation: After a preposition such as to, use the object form: me.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: My wife and I are travelling on Monday.
Me and my wife are travelling on Monday.
items.explanation: Before the verb, use the subject form: my wife and I.

items.question: Your card is ready. You can collect ____ from the branch.
items.explanation: One card = it.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The documents? I have received it.
The documents? I have received them.
items.explanation: Documents is plural, so use them.

items.question: Mr Perera called. ____ wants to change his policy.
items.explanation: Mr = he. Keep he and his consistent.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
items.explanation: Your = belonging to you. You're = you are.

items.question: Could you tell ____ your date of birth, please?
items.explanation: After the verb tell, use the object form: me.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We will refund the full amount to you.
We will refund the full amount to yourself.
items.explanation: Use plain you. Yourself is only for “you did it to you”.

items.question: Our driver will meet ____ at arrivals.
items.explanation: After the verb meet, use the object form: you.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Please call my colleague or I.
Please call my colleague or me.
items.explanation: After a verb such as call, use the object form: me.

items.question: The app has a new design. ____ is easier to use now.
items.explanation: One app = it. Its shows possession (its design).

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
items.explanation: Possessive pronouns have no apostrophe: yours, ours, theirs.

items.question: The passengers are waiting. Could you help ____ with their bags?
items.explanation: After the verb help, use the object form: them.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
items.explanation: In a spoken question, use who, and put should before I.

items.question: Mrs Silva, your claim has been approved. We'll pay ____ on Monday.
items.explanation: After the verb pay, use the object form: you.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The tourists enjoyed themselves at the safari.
The tourists enjoyed theirselves at the safari.
The tourists enjoyed them at the safari.
items.explanation: The plural reflexive is themselves. “Theirselves” is not a word.

items.question: These seats are reserved. ____ are for the family in row 3.
items.explanation: Before the verb, use the subject form: they.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Let us check that for you.
Let we check that for you.
items.explanation: After let, use the object form: let us, let me.

sets.title: Verbs
explanation: What it is: A verb is the action or state word: check, send, pay, call (actions); be, have, know, need, understand (states).

Its job: Every sentence needs a verb. Helping verbs (do, be, have) build questions and tenses. The polite modals can, could, would, may and will turn a demand into a request or a promise. State verbs such as know, have (own) and understand don't usually take -ing.
examples: I'll check your balance now.
Could you confirm your NIC number, please?
Your policy covers hospital stays.
I understand how frustrating this is.

sayThis.say: I have a question about my bill.
sayThis.why: Have (own) is a state verb: no -ing. And ask a question; a doubt means you think something may be untrue.

items.question: I ____ a question about my statement.
items.explanation: Have (own) is a state verb, so no -ing. Say question, not doubt.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Did you went to the branch yesterday?
Did you go to the branch yesterday?
items.explanation: After did, use the base verb: go.

items.question: I'm sorry, I ____ the answer, but I'll find out.
items.explanation: Know is a state verb: I don't know.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We can able to help you today.
We are able to help you today.
We can able help you today.
items.explanation: Use can or be able to, never both together.

items.question: Polite request: ____ I have your account number, please?
items.explanation: May I…? is a polite request. Must and should sound like orders or advice.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Please explain the charges to me.
items.explanation: You explain something to someone.

items.question: The policy ____ hospital stays up to 30 days.
items.explanation: The policy = it, so covers. It's a fixed fact, so use the present simple.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Could you please sign and return the form?
items.explanation: Say exactly what you need. “Do the needful” is vague to many customers.

items.question: Our agent will ____ to you by 3 p.m.
items.explanation: Get back to you is the natural phrase. Revert means go back to an earlier state.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He doesn't have the reference number.
He don't have the reference number.
He doesn't has the reference number.
items.explanation: He + doesn't + the base verb: have.

items.question: I ____ your frustration, sir.
items.explanation: Understand is a state verb: I understand.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Can we prepone the meeting to Monday?
Can we bring the meeting forward to Monday?
items.explanation: Prepone is not understood outside South Asia. Say bring forward.

items.question: The tour ____ at 6 a.m. tomorrow.
items.explanation: A timetable uses the present simple. The tour = it, so starts.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
items.explanation: Include is an ordinary verb, so the question uses does.

items.question: The driver ____ waiting outside the hotel.
items.explanation: The driver = he or she, so is + waiting.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I will discuss about it with my manager.
I will discuss it with my manager.
items.explanation: Discuss takes no preposition.

items.question: Could you ____ me the OTP you just received?
items.explanation: Tell someone something. Say something (to someone).

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We would like to apologise for the delay.
We would like to apologising for the delay.
items.explanation: Would like to + the base verb: apologise.

items.question: Your claim ____ approved this morning.
items.explanation: One claim, finished time (this morning): was approved.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I must to check with the supervisor.
I need to check with the supervisor.
I need check with the supervisor.
items.explanation: Need to + verb. Must takes no to.

sets.title: Adjectives
explanation: What it is: An adjective describes a noun: a quick reply, a safe journey, a valid ticket, a worried customer.

Its job: Adjectives go before a noun or after be, feel, look or seem. They add the detail and warmth customers notice. To compare, use -er or more (faster, more convenient); for the top one, use -est or most (the cheapest, the most popular), never both.
examples: Your new card will arrive in three working days.
Thank you for your patience. That was a long wait.
The beach is quieter in the morning.
It's the most popular tour we offer.

sayThis.say: This plan is better for you.
sayThis.not: This plan is more better for you.
sayThis.why: Better is already a comparison, so don't add more.

items.question: The express service is ____ than the standard one.
items.explanation: Short adjective + -er + than: faster than. Never more + -er.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: This is the most cheapest room we have.
This is the cheapest room we have.
items.explanation: Use -est or most, never both.

items.question: I'm ____ that you had to wait so long.
items.explanation: After be, use the adjective: I'm sorry.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We offer a two-day tour of Kandy.
We offer a two-days tour of Kandy.
items.explanation: Number + noun before another noun stays singular: a two-day tour.

items.question: The customer was very ____ because the flight was cancelled.
items.explanation: #NAME?

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
items.explanation: The tour causes the feeling, so -ing: interesting.

items.question: Your policy is ____ until 31 December.
items.explanation: After is, use the adjective: valid.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I am very much happy with the service.
I am very happy with the service.
items.explanation: Very + adjective. Very much goes with verbs: thank you very much.

items.question: Is now a ____ time to talk?
items.explanation: Good is the adjective before a noun. Well is the adverb.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: She is elder than her brother.
She is older than her brother.
items.explanation: Use older with than. Elder only goes before a noun: my elder sister.

items.question: We have a ____ room with a sea view.
items.explanation: Before a noun, use the plain adjective: a large room.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The room was enough big for the family.
The room was big enough for the family.
items.explanation: Enough goes after the adjective: big enough.

items.question: The new app is ____ to use than the old one.
items.explanation: Comparing two things with than: easier.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
items.explanation: After is, use the adjective: active.

items.question: This is the ____ beach on the south coast.
items.explanation: Long adjectives use most for the top one: the most beautiful.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We had a very bad experience.
We had a very badly experience.
items.explanation: Before a noun, use the adjective: bad.

items.question: Please keep your ____ items in the room safe.
items.explanation: Before the noun items, use the adjective: valuable.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I am confusing about the charges.
I am confused about the charges.
items.explanation: A person feels confused. Confusing describes the charges.

items.question: Sorry, the line is not very ____. Could you repeat that?
items.explanation: After is, use the adjective: clear.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The hotel is a short walk from the station.
The hotel is a shortly walk from the station.
items.explanation: Before the noun walk, use the adjective: short.

sets.title: Present tenses
explanation: What it is: Tenses show when something happens. The present tenses cover facts, what is happening now, and past actions that matter now.

Its job: Choose the tense by its job on the call. A fact or policy uses the present simple. Something happening right now uses the present continuous. An update with a result now uses the present perfect. A common slip is overusing -ing for facts and states.
## Present simple
Form: I/you/we/they check; he/she/it checks. Questions and negatives: do/does + base verb.
When to use it: Facts, policies, prices, routines and timetables. Also state verbs: know, have, need, understand.
Call examples: The policy covers outpatient care up to Rs 50,000. / The train to Ella leaves at 8.30. / Does the price include tax?
Common slips: “He don't”, “The bank close at 3” (missing -s), “I am staying in Kandy” for where you live.
## Present continuous
Form: am/is/are + verb-ing.
When to use it: What is happening right now, temporary situations, and fixed near-future arrangements.
Call examples: I'm checking your account now. / We're experiencing high call volumes. / The driver is waiting at gate 2.
Common slips: Overusing it for facts and states: “I am having a doubt”, “I am knowing”, “We are providing free Wi-Fi”.
## Present perfect
Form: have/has + past participle (sent, received, paid).
When to use it: An action in the past with a result now, with no finished time. Updates: just, already, yet, ever, since, for.
Call examples: I've just sent you the link. / We've received your claim. / Have you received the OTP yet?
Common slips: Using it with a finished time: “I have sent it yesterday”. Using the present for duration: “I am working here since 2020”.
## Present perfect continuous (briefly)
Form: have/has been + verb-ing.
When to use it: An activity that started in the past and is still going, often with how long.
Call examples: I've been trying to reach you since Monday. / You've been waiting for 20 minutes. I'm sorry.
Common slips: “I am waiting since morning” instead of “I've been waiting since this morning”.
examples: Our branch opens at 9 a.m. (present simple: a timetable)
I'm checking your account now. (present continuous: right now)
I've just sent you the link. (present perfect: the result is now)
You've been waiting 20 minutes; I'm sorry. (present perfect continuous: still going)

sayThis.say: We provide free Wi-Fi in all rooms.
sayThis.not: We are providing free Wi-Fi in all rooms.
sayThis.why: A permanent service is a fact, so use the present simple.

items.question: Sorry for the silence, I ____ the issue now.
items.explanation: Happening at this moment: present continuous.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Our branch opens at 9 a.m. on weekdays.
Our branch is opening at 9 a.m. on weekdays.
items.explanation: A regular timetable uses the present simple.

items.question: I ____ waiting since 10 o'clock.
items.explanation: Started in the past and still going, with since: present perfect continuous.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I have sent the documents yesterday.
items.explanation: A finished time (yesterday) takes the past simple, not the present perfect.

items.question: The policy ____ outpatient care.
items.explanation: A fixed fact about the policy: present simple, with -s for it.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I have a question about my bill.
I am having a question about my bill.
items.explanation: Have (own) is a state verb, so no -ing.

items.question: We've just ____ your claim.
items.explanation: Present perfect: have + the past participle, received.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He works here for five years.
He has worked here for five years.
He is working here since five years.
items.explanation: From the past until now with for: present perfect.

items.question: ____ you received the OTP yet?
items.explanation: Yet + the past participle received: Have you received…?

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We are experiencing high call volumes right now.
We experience high call volumes right now.
items.explanation: A temporary situation right now: present continuous.

items.question: Mr Fernando ____ in Galle, but this week he is staying in Colombo.
items.explanation: A permanent home uses the present simple; the temporary stay uses the continuous.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
items.explanation: A fact about the price: present simple, with does in the question.

items.question: The driver ____ for you at the arrivals gate right now.
items.explanation: Right now: present continuous.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
items.explanation: Already goes between have and the past participle.

items.question: How long ____ you been a customer with us?
items.explanation: How long + from the past until now: have you been.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: She doesn't need a visa for Sri Lanka.
She don't need a visa for Sri Lanka.
She isn't needing a visa for Sri Lanka.
items.explanation: She + doesn't + base verb. Need is a state verb, so no -ing.

items.question: We ____ free Wi-Fi in all rooms.
items.explanation: A permanent service: present simple. We takes provide, without -s.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I am trying to call you since Monday.
I have been trying to call you since Monday.
items.explanation: Since Monday and still going: present perfect continuous.

items.question: The system ____ down at the moment, so I can't see your balance.
items.explanation: The system = it, so is.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
items.explanation: Ever + life experience: Have you ever + past participle?

sessions.title: Linking words into conversation
sessions.intro: Adverbs, articles, prepositions and connectors, then the past and future tenses, including will and going to for the commitments you make on every call.

sets.title: Adverbs
explanation: What it is: An adverb describes a verb, an adjective or a whole sentence: quickly, carefully, already, today, usually, really, unfortunately.

Its job: Adverbs tell the customer how, when, where or how often. Many end in -ly. Frequency adverbs (always, usually) and already, just and still go before the main verb. Time words (today, soon) usually go at the end.
examples: I'll call you back shortly.
Please drive carefully. The road is wet.
Your refund has already been processed.
We usually reply within 24 hours.

sayThis.say: I'll call you back later today.
sayThis.not: I'll call you back today itself.
sayThis.why: “Itself” adds nothing. For emphasis, give a time: before 5 p.m.

items.question: Please speak ____; the line is not clear.
items.explanation: An adverb describes how you speak: slowly.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I will send it today itself.
items.explanation: “Today itself” is a local habit. Say today, or give a time.

items.question: We ____ reply within 24 hours.
items.explanation: A frequency adverb goes before the main verb, and it's spelt with -ll-.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The agent handled the complaint very good.
The agent handled the complaint very well.
items.explanation: Well is the adverb of good: handled it well.

items.question: Your card has ____ been dispatched.
items.explanation: Already is for positive sentences. Yet is for questions and negatives.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
items.explanation: In a negative sentence, use yet at the end.

items.question: Please drive ____. The road to Ella has many bends.
items.explanation: An adverb describes how you drive: carefully.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I always check the details twice.
I check always the details twice.
items.explanation: A frequency adverb goes before the main verb.

items.question: The bus is ____ late. It should be here in five minutes.
items.explanation: An adverb describes the adjective late: slightly late.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Even I had the same problem last month.
I had the same problem last month too.
items.explanation: “Even I” sounds surprised. For “me too”, use too or also.

items.question: I'm ____ sorry for the confusion.
items.explanation: An adverb strengthens the adjective sorry: really sorry.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He drives fast-fast, so please ask him to slow down.
He drives very fast, so please ask him to slow down.
items.explanation: Don't double a word for emphasis. Use very.

items.question: The hotel is ____ ten minutes from the airport.
items.explanation: About (or around) + a number, with no extra preposition.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
items.explanation: Soon is already an adverb. “Soonly” is not a word.

items.question: Your claim is ____ being reviewed.
items.explanation: Still = it continues now.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
items.explanation: An adverb comments on the whole sentence: Unfortunately,…

items.question: The payment went through ____.
items.explanation: An adverb describes how it went: successfully.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I'll call you back immediately itself.
I'll call you back right away.
items.explanation: Right away or immediately. Don't add itself.

items.question: She speaks English very ____.
items.explanation: Speaks how? Well (the adverb).

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Have you ever been to Yala?
Have you been ever to Yala?
items.explanation: Ever goes before the past participle: have you ever been.

sets.title: Articles
explanation: What it is: The articles are a, an and the. They are small words, which is why they are often dropped.

Its job: A or an means one of many: a form, an hour (an before a vowel sound). The means the one we both know: the form I sent you. Use no article for things in general (customers like chat) and most place names (Colombo, Sri Lanka).
examples: I'll send you an OTP by SMS.
The link expires in an hour.
Could you open the email I sent?
Kandy is a beautiful city.

sayThis.say: Could you fill in the form, please?
sayThis.why: A singular countable noun needs a, an or the.

items.question: I'll send you ____ OTP now.
items.explanation: OTP starts with a vowel sound (“oh”), so an.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Could you fill in the form, please?
items.explanation: Form is singular and countable, so it needs an article: the form.

items.question: The transfer will take about ____ hour.
items.explanation: The h in hour is silent, so an hour.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
items.explanation: University starts with a “you” sound, so a.

items.question: Could you open ____ email I sent this morning?
items.explanation: We both know which email, so the.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We will visit the Kandy tomorrow.
items.explanation: Most city names take no article.

items.question: Is there ____ ATM near the hotel?
items.explanation: ATM starts with a vowel sound (“ay”), so an.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I need copy of your NIC.
I need a copy of your NIC.
items.explanation: Copy is singular and countable, so a copy.

items.question: ____ nature in Sri Lanka is beautiful.
items.explanation: Nature in general takes no article.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Your driver is on the way.
items.explanation: The fixed phrase is on the way.

items.question: We have ____ office in Galle and two in Colombo.
items.explanation: One of several offices, before a vowel sound: an office.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
items.explanation: European starts with a “you” sound, so a.

items.question: This is ____ best offer we have this month.
items.explanation: Superlatives take the: the best.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
items.explanation: SMS starts with the sound “es”, so an.

items.question: Our agent will call you in ____ morning.
items.explanation: The fixed phrase is in the morning.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
items.explanation: The h in honest is silent, so an.

items.question: Could you spell ____ name of the street?
items.explanation: A specific name we both mean: the name of the street.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We arranged a taxi for you.
items.explanation: Taxi is singular and countable, so a taxi.

items.question: There is ____ problem with your payment.
items.explanation: Mentioning it for the first time, before a consonant sound: a problem.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The Sri Lanka is famous for tea.
Sri Lanka is famous for tea.
items.explanation: Most country names take no article.

sets.title: Prepositions
explanation: What it is: Prepositions are small linking words for place, time and relationships: in, on, at, to, for, from, with, about.

Its job: They connect a noun to the rest of the sentence. Time: at 3 p.m., on Monday, in March. Many verbs and adjectives have a fixed partner (interested in, pay for, depend on), and some verbs take none (discuss, contact, reach).
examples: Your appointment is on Monday at 10 a.m.
The pick-up is at the main entrance.
I'm calling about your claim.
Thank you for waiting.

sayThis.why: Discuss takes no preposition (but talk about).

items.question: Your appointment is ____ Monday.
items.explanation: Days take on.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.

sets.title: Conjunctions and connectors
explanation: What it is: Conjunctions and connectors join ideas: and, but, or, because, so, although, however, if, unless, until.

Its job: They show the customer how two ideas relate: a reason (because), a result (so), a contrast (but, although, however) or a condition (if, unless). Use one connector per link: because or so, although or but, never both.
examples: I can't see the payment yet because it takes one working day to clear.
The road is closed, so we'll take the coast road.
The room is small; however, it has a sea view.
If you send the receipt today, we can pay by Friday.

sayThis.say: Because the system is down, I can't check it.
sayThis.not: Because the system is down, so I can't check it.
sayThis.why: Use because or so, not both.

items.explanation: After if, use the present simple, not will.

items.question: I understand you're upset, ____ I'll do my best to fix this today.
items.explanation: And adds the next idea: empathy, then action.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The claim was rejected as the policy had lapsed.
The claim was rejected as because the policy had lapsed.
items.explanation: Use as or because, not both.

sets.title: Past and future tenses
explanation: What it is: The past tenses tell the customer what happened. The future forms tell them what will happen next, and on a call that usually means a commitment.

Its job: Use the past simple for finished events at a finished time. Use the past continuous for background, and the past perfect for the earlier of two past events. For commitments, use will + a clear time. Use going to for plans that are already decided.
## Past simple
Form: verb-ed or the irregular form (went, sent, paid). Questions and negatives: did + base verb.
When to use it: Finished actions at a finished time (yesterday, on Monday, at 10.15). Telling the customer what happened.
Call examples: The payment went through at 10.15. / Did you receive the SMS? / We didn't receive your form.
Common slips: “Did you went”, “I came yesterday itself”, “Yesterday I am going”.
## Past continuous
Form: was/were + verb-ing.
When to use it: The background action in the past, often interrupted by a shorter one.
Call examples: I was checking your file when the line dropped. / The driver was waiting at the wrong gate.
Common slips: “I was waiting since morning” (use I've been waiting, or I had been waiting).
## Past perfect
Form: had + past participle.
When to use it: The earlier of two past events.
Call examples: By the time you called, we had already sent the refund. / The policy had lapsed before the accident.
Common slips: Using it for a simple past event: “I had called you yesterday.”
## Past perfect continuous (briefly)
Form: had been + verb-ing.
When to use it: A long activity up to a moment in the past.
Call examples: She had been waiting for an hour when the taxi arrived.
Common slips: “She was waiting since an hour.”
## Future: will
Form: will + base verb (I'll, we'll).
When to use it: Promises, offers, commitments and decisions made on the call. Always add a time.
Call examples: I'll call you back by 3 p.m. / We'll email you the receipt right away.
Common slips: “I will revert back”, “I'll do one thing”, and a promise with no time.
## Future: going to
Form: am/is/are going to + base verb.
When to use it: Plans already decided before the call, and predictions from what you can see.
Call examples: We're going to replace the router tomorrow; the technician is booked. / It's going to rain, so take an umbrella.
Common slips: Dropping be: “We going to send it.”
## Future continuous
Form: will be + verb-ing.
When to use it: Something in progress at a future time, and a soft, polite question.
Call examples: Our driver will be waiting at arrivals. / Will you be using the card abroad?
Common slips: Using it for promises: “I will be calling you” sounds vague. Say “I'll call you at 4.”
## Future perfect
Form: will have + past participle.
When to use it: Something finished before a future time.
Call examples: By the time you land, we'll have prepared your room. / By Friday, the refund will have reached your account.
Common slips: “By Friday we will finish it” when you mean it will be done before Friday.
## Future perfect continuous (briefly)
Form: will have been + verb-ing.
When to use it: How long something will have gone on by a future time.
Call examples: By June, you'll have been paying the loan for two years.
Common slips: Rare on calls. Recognise it, but don't force it.
examples: You called us on Monday. (past simple)
I was checking your file when the line dropped. (past continuous)
By the time you called, we had already sent the refund. (past perfect)
I'll call you back by 3 p.m. today. (will: a commitment)

sayThis.say: I'll call you back by 3 p.m. today.
sayThis.why: A commitment needs will + a clear action + a time.

sessions.title: Vowels and clear speech
sessions.intro: An introduction to vowels: letters versus sounds, a versus an, short and long sounds, and the vowel pairs that change meaning on a call. On the phone the customer only hears you, so one vowel can turn a bill into a bell.

sets.title: Vowel letters, vowel sounds, and a or an
explanation: What it is: English has five vowel letters (a, e, i, o, u) but about 20 vowel sounds. The letters are what you write; the sounds are what the customer hears.

Its job: Vowel sounds carry the meaning of a word, and they decide a or an. Choose by the first sound, not the first letter: an before a vowel sound (an hour, an MBA, an SMS), a before a consonant sound (a university, a one-time code, a European tour). The word the changes too: it sounds like “thee” before a vowel sound (the airport) and “thuh” before a consonant (the bank).
## Letter versus sound
hour: an hour
university: a university
MBA: an MBA
one-time code: a one-time code
SMS: an SMS
European: a European tour
examples: I'll send you an SMS with a one-time code.
Your call will be returned within an hour.
She has an MBA and a university degree in finance.
Is there an ATM near the hotel?

sayThis.say: I'll send you a one-time code.
sayThis.not: I'll send you an one-time code.
sayThis.why: One starts with a “w” sound, so a.

sets.title: Short and long vowels
explanation: What it is: Many English vowels come in short and long pairs: ship/sheep, live/leave, fill/feel, full/fool, pull/pool.

Its job: The long sound is held longer and the mouth is tighter: spread your lips for “ee” and round them for “oo”. The short sound is quick and relaxed. Spelling gives clues: ee and ea are usually long (seat, leave), while oo can be short (book, look, good) or long (food, pool, room).
## Short and long pairs
ship: The ship leaves at 6 p.m.
live: Please leave your bags here.
fill: Please fill in this form.
sit: Your seat is 14A.
full: Sorry, the hotel is full.
pull: The pool closes at 8.
examples: Please leave your key at reception when you check out. (long “ee”)
Do you live in Colombo? (short “i”)
The pool opens at 7 a.m. (long “oo”)
Please pull the door; it's heavy. (short “oo”, as in full)

sayThis.say: Please leave the key at reception. (long “ee”)
sayThis.not: Please live the key at reception. (short “i”)
sayThis.why: Leave (long ee) means go or put down; live (short i) means have your home.

sets.title: Meaning-changing pairs and Sri Lankan vowel slips
explanation: What it is: Some words differ by only one vowel sound. On a call the customer can't see your face or your spelling, so one wrong vowel can change the meaning.

Its job: Learn the pairs that matter in your job: bill/bell, sit/seat, pull/pool, cost/coast, bed/bad, men/man, walk/work, date/debt, law/low, cup/cap. Common Sri Lankan English slips: mixing the a and e sounds (bad/bed, man/men), merging walk and work, using a short vowel in a long word (sit for seat), shortening long “ay” and “oh” (date, coast), and adding a vowel before s + consonant (“iskool” for school, “istation” for station).
## Pairs that change meaning on calls
bill / bell: I'll send you the bill.
cost / coast: The coast road costs less.
bed / bad: A double bed, not a bad room.
work / walk: We work until 5; it's a short walk.
date / debt: Your date of birth, please.
law / low: Your balance is low.
examples: I'll email you the bill this evening. (not bell)
The coast road is closed, so the trip will cost a little more.
Our team works until 5 p.m.; it's a short walk from the station.
Would you like a double bed? We had a bad line earlier, sorry.

sayThis.say: School, station, staff: start straight on the s.
sayThis.why: Don't add a vowel before s + a consonant.

items.explanation: Bill (short i) is what you pay. Bell (short e) rings.

placement.question: Choose the correct sentence.
